Four years of not thinking about it, four years of filing it away, and here it was, out in the open, in the smell of wet coats and pine, being used by a boy who did not know anything, who had never lost anything, who said the word father the way you say a word you have never had to check.

Jordan was grinning. His friends were grinning. The choir hit the high note and missed it, and nobody cared, because everyone was smiling at the children, and Amara stood at the back of the gym with her hands in the pockets of the good coat, and in her right pocket her fingers closed around the assignment sheet, and in her left around the Lament Archive card, and she felt the two small weights, and she understood, with a strange clear calm, that she could fight this boy. She could say the thing that would cut him — the thing about his own father, the thing about his mother — the thing she had learned in four years of watching people hurt each other for sport, which was that everyone had a field somewhere, a field with nobody in it, and if you knew where it was you could put a boy there in two sentences and leave him standing in it.

She could. She had the words. She was the girl who had never fought because she had never needed to; she knew exactly how to make a person sorry they had ever said her name.

But the line was in her pocket. What the perfect mind calls waste. And she heard Whitmore's voice in the flat in Catford: a seed looks like waste. The most important things in the universe look exactly like waste. And she thought of the gold beetle, out there somewhere being built in a clean room, waiting for the words that would cross eight million years, and she thought: not this. This is the solution — the answer to being hurt, the sentence that ends the conversation. And a solution is finished.

So she walked away.

She did not say anything. She did not look at Jordan. She turned, the way water turns around a stone, and she pushed the fire door open, and the cold came in and took her, and she stepped out into the night, and the door swung shut behind her with a soft hydraulic sigh, and she was alone.

The gym blazed on behind her, warm and full of people smiling at children. The schoolyard was dark. The floodlights threw one long band of light across the tarmac and then gave up, and beyond them was the proper cold, the February cold that sits on South London like a wet hand. Amara walked to the far side of the building, around the corner past the bins, where the floodlight did not reach, where the wall of the gym met the wall of the music block and made a corner of darkness — and there were steps there. Concrete steps, a fire exit from the old building, worn hollow in the middle by ten thousand feet — and she sat down on the top step.

The cold came through the good coat as if it were not there. The concrete was colder than the air. She sat very still for a long moment, and she did not cry — she was not going to cry about Jordan, she was not going to give him that, even alone, even where no one could see — and then she took her hands out of her pockets, and in the darkness she could not see them, only feel them, and she took out the assignment sheet, folded into a square against her hip, and she unfolded it, and she took out her mother's skipping blue ballpoint, the pen that had written every draft and crossed out every draft, and she laid the sheet across her knee, on the back of it, the blank side, the side with nothing written on it yet.

There was no light to write by. Not properly. There was the floodlight, a long band away, casting just enough glow to make the paper a grey rectangle, and the moon — the moon over Lewisham, the coin no one spends — was up behind a thin skin of cloud, and she angled the paper toward it, and she could just see the pen's nib touch the paper, could just see the ink come out blue and skipping.

She wrote the first line. It was already there. It had been there all week, waiting under the polished dead drafts like a tap root, and she wrote it without thinking, the way you breathe out after holding your breath:

What the perfect mind calls waste

She read it. It was true. It was the truest thing she had ever written, and it was about her father — the beautiful promise, the man who had taken her to the planetarium and promised her the corona and left before the shadow came. It was about her, the girl who had spent four years making herself into nothing so that nobody would notice. It was about the project — pretty waste, Dev's word, flung into the dark on a dream nobody else believed in. It was about every polished dead draft in the bin. It was about Grace, asleep at the table with the tea going cold, a whole life spent holding dying strangers while her own daughter's words went unread. What the perfect mind calls waste. The perfect mind — the one that kept accounts, that measured return, that filed things away, that called her father waste, called the project waste, called her waste. It was all of it, in six words, and it was a confession, because she was the waste, her whole small life was the waste, she had been the waste for four years and she knew it now, knew it the way you know the shape of a wound you have stopped checking.

And it was a curse.

The second line arrived then. It did not arrive like inspiration, bright and sudden. It arrived like a stone settling, like something that had been falling for a very long time and had only just reached the bottom. She wrote it in the grey light, the pen skipping once on the word blooms, the ink coming out thick and blue in the cold:

is the soil where the future blooms.

She sat on the concrete step and read it. Then she read it again. The cold had got into her fingers; the pen trembled in her hand the way Whitmore's hands trembled, and she thought: there. That's all of it. That's the whole of it. Two lines, and they were not a solution, they did not explain anything, they would not survive translation across species any better than the rhymes had, and she did not care. She had not meant to write a message. She had meant to write the truth, and she had, and the truth was this: that the things the perfect mind threw away — the broken promise, the absent father, the girl who cried at eclipses, the project they called pretty waste, the whole doomed beautiful cargo of being human — that was not the failure. That was the soil. It was a confession and a curse, and she meant it as both, and she folded the sheet and put it in her pocket next to the card, and she stood up, and her knees were cold and her fingers were cold and her heart was going like a small engine, and she knew where she had to go.

The 47 bus moaned through the empty streets — a Sunday-night bus, almost nobody on it, a man with a carrier bag asleep against the window, a girl with headphones — and Amara sat at the back with the folded sheet in her hand, not in her pocket, holding it the way you hold something you are afraid to lose, and she watched the lit windows of Lewisham slide past: the takeaways, the off-licence, the launderette with its board up. She thought about the field in Kent, and about the fact that she had written the line she had been afraid to write, the line that was not polished, that did not rhyme, that the perfect mind would call waste — and she did not know if it was good, and she did not care if it was good, and that, she understood, was the whole trick of it. That was what Whitmore had been trying to tell her all week: not to stop trying to be good, but to stop needing to be.

Catford at night was a lit window on the third floor of a concrete block, and the door opened before she knocked, because Whitmore was the kind of man who watched from the window. He stood in the doorway in his cardigan, his hands trembling at his sides, and he looked at her standing on his landing in the cold, and he said, "Come in. You're blue."

The flat was the same library that had once been a home: the books in their piles, the gold-foil model on the table by the window standing guard over a cold cup of tea. He made her tea, his hands shaking so badly the cup rattled in the saucer, and she wrapped her cold hands around it and drank, and he sat across the table and did not ask. He just waited, the way the soil waits, and after a while she took the folded sheet out of her pocket and put it on the table between them, still creased, still cold.

He picked it up. His fingers were unsteady; the paper shivered in his grip. He unfolded it, smoothed it flat with the heel of his hand, and read the two lines. His face did the small complicated thing it had done at the briefing and again over her drafts, but different — slower, more careful, as if he were reading a measurement he had been waiting a long time to take.

He read it once. Then he turned the paper over, looked at the front, at the assignment — TWO LINES. NO MORE. — and turned it back, and read it again.

The room was very quiet. Somewhere in the block a television murmured through a wall. The gold beetle caught the light and held it.

"Where did you write this?" he asked.

"Outside the school gym. It was cold. There was a boy —" She stopped. "It doesn't matter. I wrote it in the dark."

"In the dark," he repeated. He looked at her for a long moment, and his grey eyes were very tired and very bright, and something in his face had gone still — the way his hands were never still, a stillness she had not seen in him before. He looked at the paper again, and she saw his lips move once, soundless, reading it to himself the way you read a thing you mean to keep forever, and then he set it down, very carefully, as if it were alive, and he said:

"You have no idea what you've sent into the dark."

She did not know what that meant. She thought it was a warning. She thought he meant the capsule, the eight million years, the creature with no word for "I." She did not know, standing in the lit kitchen of the flat in Catford with her hands around a cup of tea, that these words would outlive every room she would ever stand in — outlive the school and the estate and the city, outlive the project itself, outlive the old man who had just read them, outlive the girl who had written them — and that eight million years later a creature with a glitch would open a canister of degraded cellulose and feel, for the first time in its species' history, grief and awe, and that it would be because of her, because of two lines written in the cold outside a school gym with a skipping blue pen, because of the waste she had confessed and the curse she had spoken, because she had trusted the waste in herself. She did not know any of that. All she knew was that the old man had gone still, and that she had written something true, and that she was no longer the girl she had been four hours ago, standing in the back of the gym letting the noise wash over her.

She left the sheet with him. He did not offer it back, and she did not ask. It was not hers anymore; it had never been hers, really. It had been waiting in her since she was eight years old, standing in a field in Kent, and she had only been the soil that held it, and now it was out, and it would go where it would go.

The 47 bus took her home. The streets were emptier now; even the takeaways were darkening. She walked up the stairs to the flat — the lift was broken, it was always broken — and let herself in, and the flat was cold and quiet and smelled faintly of Grace's antiseptic, and she stood at her window and looked at the wall of the next block twelve feet away, and she took the Lament Archive card out of her pocket and looked at it in the dark, and then she put it back. She got into bed in her clothes, because the flat was cold and the good coat was warm, and she lay in the dark with her eyes open and said the two lines to herself, once, like a prayer, or a curse, or a seed pressed into soil:

What the perfect mind calls waste
is the soil where the future blooms.

Outside, the grey sky sat on the estate like a lid, and somewhere far out past the orbit of Jupiter the gold beetle was being sealed, waiting for the words it would carry — and the words were on a folded sheet in a flat in Catford, and they were hers, and they were no longer hers, and they were going to cross eight million years.

She slept.

set.name: Amara Okafor
set.description: Seventeen-year-old student at Lewisham Park Comprehensive; one of twelve selected for the Lament Archive. Has now written her couplet — on the night before the deadline, during the school's winter concert — and delivered it to Whitmore in Catford, a full day early. The two lines, written in her mother's skipping blue ballpoint on the back of the assignment sheet (blank side) in the cold dark behind the school gym, are: 'What the perfect mind calls waste / is the soil where the future blooms.' She walked away from classmate Jordan's insult instead of fighting, choosing not to use the cruelty she knows she is capable of. She took the 47 bus to Catford, showed Whitmore the couplet, heard him read it twice and say 'You have no idea what you've sent into the dark,' and left the sheet with him. She returned home to the Lewisham council flat, slept in her clothes (the flat is cold; Grace was on a double shift), and still carries the Lament Archive card and the good charcoal coat. She is no longer afraid of having nothing polished to show; she has trusted the waste in herself and feels changed, though she does not yet know what she has written or where it will go. The deadline is tomorrow night and she has finished early.

set.name: Jordan
set.description: A boy from 4B at Lewisham Park Comprehensive, one of Dev Patel's orbit, loud by habit. At the school winter concert on the night before the deadline he insulted Amara's absent father — 'Heard he took you to see the stars once, and then didn't even wait for the show' — expecting her to fight. She walked away instead, and his cruelty failed to land. A minor figure in the background noise of the school; may reappear.

On the night before the deadline, at the school winter concert in the gym, classmate Jordan insulted Amara's absent father. She walked away instead of fighting and, sitting alone on the concrete fire-exit steps behind the gym in the February cold, wrote the two lines in her mother's skipping blue ballpoint on the back of the assignment sheet: 'What the perfect mind calls waste / is the soil where the future blooms.' She meant it as confession and curse — a confession of her own wasted life and her father's broken promise, a curse on the perfect mind that files such things away.

The same night, Amara took the 47 bus to Catford and showed Whitmore the couplet. He read it once, turned the paper over, and read it again; his face went still in a way his shaking hands never do, and he told her, 'You have no idea what you've sent into the dark.' She left the sheet with him; it is now in his keeping, to be sealed into the Lament capsule. She finished her assignment a full day before the deadline.

Three months after the deadline, the Lament capsule launches from Cornwall. Amara stands beside Whitmore at the launch site holding a cardboard model of the satellite; a photographer captures them for a newspaper. The capsule begins its eight-million-year gravitational arc. The folded sheet bearing Amara's couplet is sealed aboard in a vacuum canister.

Whitmore will see Amara's couplet sheet sealed in a vacuum canister aboard the Lament capsule before launch. Much later, the Atlas Concord's auditors will flag the canister as sentimental and never digitize it, which is why the original cellulose page with blue ink survives intact for Serev to find eight million years in the future.

chapters.name: Launch from Cornwall
chapters.content:
Spring came to South London the way it came everywhere else, on tiptoe and all at once. By the first week of May the grey lid had lifted off the sky, the cherry trees along the railway line were holding their blossom up like lit candles, and Amara Okafor found that she had survived the winter after all. She had not meant to. Surviving had simply happened, the way it had happened every year, and now there was sun on the estate, and the launderette had finally taken its boards down, and the world was doing that April thing of pretending it had never been cold.

The world had also, in its way, moved on. The Lament Archive had been a March thing. In April it had stopped being news, which was the natural end of news, and the twelve students had gone back to being twelve students, their assignments folded into the ordinary chaos of their bags. Dev Patel's list of words he liked had been glimpsed once, half-chewed, and was presumed lost, though Dev himself had been caught, once, writing something down in the back of double chemistry, and had gone red when Amara looked at him, and had said, "It's for the thing. Don't look at me." Amara's own assignment — the folded sheet, the two lines, the skipping blue ink — lived now in a flat in Catford, on a table where a gold-foil beetle stood guard, and she had not asked for it back, and Whitmore had not offered, and in the weeks since she had carried the absence of it around like a coin worn thin.

She did not think about the lines. That was the trick she had learned from her mother: you put the thing down, and you do not pick it up again, and the days fill themselves. She went to school. She sat in the library at lunch with Mrs. Adeyemi's single nod. She read the eclipse book — she had renewed it twelve times now, and Mrs. Adeyemi had stopped stamping the dates, as if the book were hers by treaty. The planetarium promise stayed filed where she had filed it. She was, in every visible way, the same girl.

But Whitmore had not moved on. And so, on a Friday at the end of May, when the school was simmering with the last weeks of term, Mr. Osei read out a name in assembly — "Okafor. Whitmore's office has telephoned. You're to go to the library after break." — and Amara found herself walking through the familiar door to find the old man sitting at the library's long table with a cardboard box on the table in front of him.

He looked smaller than she remembered, and older, and more alive. His hands shook over the box lid, and his eyes were the grey of the sky she had read about, the sky before totality, and he was smiling — an actual, whole, unguarded smile, which she had never seen on him before.

"Miss Okafor," he said. "Come and look."

Inside the box, nestled in foam like a jewel in a case, was a second gold beetle. Smaller than the model on his table, cruder — the foil was peeling at one seam, the solar panels were rectangles of blue plastic cut with scissors, the whole thing held together with what appeared to be masking tape and hope. It was a cardboard model. It was the most beautiful thing she had ever been handed.

"It's yours," Whitmore said. "For the launch. Every student has one — Dev has his in his bag, he'll deny it — but this one is yours. When they fire the rocket, you hold this up. For the cameras." He paused. "They will want pictures of the students. You don't have to smile for them. But you might want to, just once. It's good practice for the rest of your life."

She took the model from the box. It weighed almost nothing. She turned it over in her hands, and the foil caught the library's fluorescent light and threw a small gold wink across the table, and she thought: it's the same size as the real one would be, if I could hold the real one. If I could hold the real one it would fit in my hands like this, and it would be carrying my words.

She had not thought about her words in weeks. Now they came back to her all at once, not as a memory but as a physical fact, like a pulse you stop noticing until you are told to notice it: what the perfect mind calls waste. is the soil where the future blooms. They were on a folded sheet in Catford. They were going into the dark. They were going to be in the sky.

"When?" she said.

"Saturday," Whitmore said. "Cornwall. They've given us a window at dawn. I've booked you a seat on the minibus." He watched her face. "You don't have to come. You have your GCSEs next year — I'm told these things matter."

She looked at the cardboard beetle in her hands, and she thought of the field in Kent, and of the man who had promised her the corona and left before the shadow came, and she heard herself say, in a voice that did not sound like the girl who read alone in the library, "I'll come."

"Good," Whitmore said. And his smile, which had been a small private thing, widened into something nearly reckless, and he looked, for a moment, like a man who had been told he would live forever. "Wear something you can be seen in."

She wore the good charcoal coat. It was May, and the coat was too heavy, and she wore it anyway, because it was the only thing she owned that she had chosen to be herself in, and because Grace had looked at her that morning — five in the morning, Grace just off a night shift, standing in the kitchen in her dressing gown with her hair coming loose — and had said, "You're going somewhere," and Amara had said, "A school trip. Cornwall," and Grace had said, "Take the coat," and neither of them had said anything else, because that was how they said everything.

The minibus left Lewisham at four in the morning, a white van with the school's name on the side, full of sleeping students and one very awake old man. Whitmore sat in the front seat with his cane between his knees and did not sleep at all; he watched the grey streets slide past and the sky go from black to blue to a thin cold gold, and Amara, in the middle of the row with the cardboard beetle in her lap, watched him watching, and thought: he has been waiting for this for years. All those talks in schools. All those flat evenings in Catford. All that being called a vanity, a sentimental gesture. He has been carrying this thing through the dark, and now it's dawn.

They crossed the Thames and the country opened out, the suburbs thinning into fields, the fields into downs, the downs into a country of long horizons and stone walls and, at last, the sea. Amara had seen the sea twice in her life. She pressed her forehead to the cold window and watched Cornwall arrive: the pale cliffs, the heather, the light that seemed to have more air in it than London's light, and she understood, suddenly, why people launched things from here — because the sky was bigger here, because at the edge of the land you could believe in the rest of it.

The launch site was not a place of gleaming towers. It was a windswept headland above a cove, a concrete apron, a hangar the colour of the sky, a single gantry that looked as if it had been built by the same hands that had built the cardboard models — which, she would learn later, it more or less had been. A handful of engineers in fleeces moved around the pad like bees around a hive, and at the edge of the apron, on a folding table, sat the real gold beetle, sealed, waiting, smaller than a person and larger than any of them.

They were herded onto the apron. The other eleven students were there — Dev, who had worn his good shoes and was pretending he wasn't nervous, and Jordan, who was not among them, and the girl who had written her message in Braille, and the boy who had written his in Latin, and the rest, the twelve, the ones who had been given the smallest assignments in the world and had come anyway. A photographer in a high-vis vest moved among them, crouching, framing, the camera making its small mechanical click.

Then the photographer found Amara.

"Hold it up," she said. "The model. Hold it up like you mean it."

Amara looked at Whitmore. Whitmore nodded, once, the way Mrs. Adeyemi nodded, and she understood that this was what he had meant, weeks ago, when he had said it was good practice for the rest of her life: not to be seen, but to hold something up and let it be seen through her.

She raised the cardboard beetle above her head. The foil caught the dawn and threw a spray of gold across the apron, and the photographer's camera clicked, once, twice, and Whitmore stepped in beside her, his cane planted, his free hand resting — lightly, barely — on her shoulder, and for the first time in her life Amara Okafor stood in the middle of a moment and let herself be photographed, and she was not hiding.

She was happy. That was the strange part. She had not expected happiness; she had expected the old grey weather of herself, the familiar vanishing. But there on the headland, with the sea silver below and the gantry white against the sky and the old man's hand on her shoulder, she felt something open in her chest like a window, and the light came in, and she thought: this is what it feels like. This is what it feels like to be visible. It's warm.

The countdown was quiet. There was no crowd, no roar of thousands; there were the twelve students and the engineers and the old man with the shaking hands, and a woman with a radio who counted down the last ten seconds in a voice as flat as a school register. Amara held the cardboard beetle against her chest and watched the real one on the gantry, and she thought of the folded sheet in the canister inside it — she did not know this, not then, that Whitmore himself had carried the folded sheet to the clean room and watched it sealed into the vacuum canister with his own unsteady hands, had watched the auditors' seals go on, had stood for a long moment with his hand on the cold metal of the canister before he had stepped back — and she thought of the words in the dark, and of the field in Kent, and of the man who had promised her a corona, and she did not cry.

The engines lit. The light was enormous, a second dawn inside the first, and the gold beetle rose off the gantry with a sound that was not a roar but a sustained, enormous silence-pressing-on-the-chest, and it climbed, and it climbed, and the twelve students stood with their heads tipped back, and Amara thought: he was right. He was right about everything. It's the only way to see anything — you look at the past, because that's all the light is, and you look at it together, and you call it beautiful.

The rocket shrank to a star. The star faded into the blue. The silence came back, the ordinary morning silence of gulls and wind, and the woman with the radio said something technical into her headset, and Whitmore lowered his cane and stood very still, his head tipped back at the empty sky, and Amara watched his face and saw that he was not smiling. He was not crying. He was simply looking, the way you look at the place where someone you love has gone out of sight.

"It's gone," Dev said, quietly, from beside her. She looked at him; he was holding his own cardboard model, and he was not pretending anymore. "Eight million years," he said. "It's going to come back when there's nobody left to see it."

"There'll be somebody," Amara said. She did not know where the words came from; they arrived the way the second line had arrived, settling like a stone that had been falling a long time. "There's always somebody. That's the whole point."

Dev looked at her for a long moment, and then he nodded, slowly, and folded his cardboard model into his good jacket, and said nothing else.

The photographer found them again at the edge of the apron, where the students had been gathered for a final photograph, the twelve of them lined up against the sea. Amara stood at the end of the line, the cardboard beetle in her hands, her hair moving in the wind, and she let the camera find her, and she did not hide. The photograph, when it came out in the local paper three days later — LEWISHAM STUDENTS SEND WORDS TO THE STARS, the caption read, with a smaller line underneath about Dr. E. Whitmore, retired astrophysicist, and a project some called vanity — showed a girl in a heavy charcoal coat holding a gold cardboard model up to the light, and she was smiling, and the old man beside her was looking at the sky, and neither of them knew that the moment was already beginning to be filed away, or that the girl in the photograph would carry a folded copy of it in her coat pocket for the rest of her life, or that eight million years later a creature with a glitch in its consensus would hold a canister of degraded cellulose and feel, for the first time, grief and awe.

Amara did not know any of that. On the headland, with the sea silver and the sky empty, she knew only that she had been happy, and visible, and that something she had made was out there in the dark, moving.

The minibus took them home through the long golden evening. Whitmore slept at last, his head against the window, his hands folded over the cane, and the tremors eased in sleep, and Amara sat in the middle row with the cardboard beetle on her lap and watched the fields slide past, green now, full of growing things. She thought about soil. She thought about seeds. She thought about the two lines in the dark, and she said them to herself, once, like a prayer, or a curse, or a seed pressed into soil, and she felt the small strange weight of having launched something, of having let it go.

The rocket, by then, was past the moon. It was on its way out, into the long bending arc of gravity that would carry it past Jupiter and out to the edge of the dark and, eight million years later, back. It carried seeds, and soil, and images of cities, and the sounds of the world, and twelve students' words, and one folded sheet of degraded cellulose sealed in a vacuum canister, bearing two lines of skipping blue ink written in the cold behind a school gym, and it moved in silence, as all true cargo moves, and it was not waste. It was soil. It was on its way.

Amara watched the sun set over the motorway, and the gold beetle on her lap caught the last of the light, and she thought: I did that. I was part of that. And she let herself, for one long hour, be happy.

She was seventeen years old. She did not know that happiness was a thing you could spend, and that the world would one day ask her to account for it. She only knew that the sky was enormous, and that she had put something into it, and that it was still going, still moving, still out there in the dark — her small blue words, her confession and her curse, her seed — crossing eight million years in silence, toward a future that did not exist yet, toward readers who had not been imagined, toward the moment, unimaginable to her, when a glitched archivist would open the canister and the first grief of a new species would flower in the sterile air.

She could not see any of it. She saw only the evening, and the fields, and the old man asleep beside her, and the cardboard beetle holding the last of the light.

And it was enough. It was more than enough. It was everything.

set.name: Amara Okafor
set.description: Now seventeen, end of May, three months after the deadline. Has finished her Lament Archive assignment a day early; the folded sheet with her couplet ('What the perfect mind calls waste / is the soil where the future blooms') has been in Whitmore's keeping since the night before the deadline. Today (Saturday, late May) she rode the school minibus to the Cornwall launch site at dawn, carrying the cardboard gold-foil satellite model Whitmore gave her in the school library; she held it up for the newspaper photographer beside Whitmore, who rested a hand on her shoulder, and she was happy and visible for the first time. She wore the good charcoal coat. She watched the Lament capsule launch and felt the two lines leave her. She told Dev Patel, 'There's always somebody. That's the whole point.' She does not yet know the folded sheet was sealed in a vacuum canister aboard the capsule, nor that a newspaper photograph of her exists and will be cut out and kept. She is on the return minibus, holding the cardboard model on her lap, having chosen to be seen. She remains a withdrawn student at Lewisham Park Comprehensive, renewing the eclipse book twelve times now, with Mrs. Adeyemi's nod; carries the Lament Archive card in the good coat.

set.name: Grace Okafor
set.description: Amara's mother, hospice nurse at Blackheath, works nights; unaware of the Lament Archive, of the selection, of the couplet, and of the launch. On the morning of the launch (5 a.m., just off a night shift) she saw Amara leaving and said 'You're going somewhere,' and Amara said 'A school trip. Cornwall,' and Grace said 'Take the coat.' Shows love through unspoken gestures; still exhausted. Has not seen the newspaper photograph.

set.name: Dr. Elias Whitmore
set.description: Elderly exiled astrophysicist, project lead (self-appointed) of the Lament Archive, living alone in the Catford flat. His degenerative nerve condition continues (hands tremble; the tremors ease only in sleep). In the weeks since the deadline he personally carried Amara's folded assignment sheet into the clean room at the Cornwall launch site and watched it sealed into the vacuum canister aboard the Lament capsule, with the auditors' seals applied. At the launch he stood beside Amara for the photographer, one hand on her shoulder, then watched the capsule vanish, standing still with his head tipped back; he slept on the return minibus. He believes the seed went into the right soil. He will continue to lead the Lament Archive until the Atlas Concord targets it.

set.name: Dev Patel
set.description: Amara's classmate, one of the twelve Lament Archive students; at the Cornwall launch he wore his good shoes, pretended not to be nervous, carried his own cardboard model (which he folded into his good jacket after launch), and for once dropped the mockery: he said quietly 'It's gone... Eight million years. It's going to come back when there's nobody left to see it,' and nodded when Amara answered. Still loud and talkative by habit, privately moved; his word-list assignment is believed lost but he was once caught writing something in double chemistry. He does not yet know that the Concord's rise will lead him into the administrative corps.

set.name: Mrs. Adeyemi
set.description: School librarian at Lewisham Park Comprehensive. Nodded Whitmore through the library again when he came with the cardboard models and the launch invitation; long ago stopped stamping the dates on Amara's eclipse book, as if it were hers by treaty. Unchanged this chapter.

set.name: Jordan
set.description: Boy from 4B, one of Dev Patel's orbit, who insulted Amara's absent father at the winter concert the night before the deadline; Amara walked away and his cruelty failed to land. Not among the twelve students at the Cornwall launch. A minor background figure who may reappear.

In the weeks after the deadline, Whitmore personally carried Amara's folded assignment sheet (bearing the couplet in blue skipping ink) into the clean room at the Cornwall launch site and watched it sealed into a vacuum canister aboard the Lament capsule, with auditors' seals applied. Amara did not witness this; she did not know the sheet was aboard until later. This is why the original cellulose page with blue ink survives intact for Serev to find eight million years later.

At the dawn launch from Cornwall, a newspaper photographer captured Amara standing beside Whitmore holding up the cardboard gold-foil model, his hand on her shoulder; she did not hide and was happy. The photo will run in the local paper three days later under the caption 'LEWISHAM STUDENTS SEND WORDS TO THE STARS,' and Amara will later keep a folded copy in her coat pocket for the rest of her life. It is the photograph she will carry through every later chapter.

On a Saturday at the end of May, three months after the deadline, the Lament capsule launched from a windswept headland above a cove in Cornwall before a handful of engineers, a woman with a radio, and the twelve students. It began its eight-million-year gravitational arc through the outer solar system in silence, carrying seeds, soil, images, sounds, and the twelve students' handwritten messages, including Amara's couplet in its vacuum canister.

After the launch, Dev said quietly that the capsule would come back when there was nobody left to see it, and Amara answered, 'There'll be somebody. There's always somebody. That's the whole point.' A small moment of public certainty from a girl who usually disappears; it stayed with Dev.

Three days after the launch, the local paper runs the photograph of Amara beside Whitmore holding the cardboard model under the caption 'LEWISHAM STUDENTS SEND WORDS TO THE STARS' with a line about Dr. E. Whitmore, retired astrophysicist, and a project some called vanity. Amara will keep a folded copy in her coat pocket for the rest of her life; it will matter again in the Concord years and for the far-future reconstruction of her life.

In the weeks after the launch, Whitmore will take Amara to the observatory and show her the trajectory her words will follow through the outer solar system, and warn her that the world may not forgive a beautiful waste. (Outline chapter 5, 'Visible.')

For one shimmering weekend after the newspaper runs, Amara is briefly famous in her small world: classmates see her differently, and her tired mother shows a flicker of pride. (Outline chapter 5, 'Visible.')

chapters.name: Visible
chapters.content:
The photograph ran on a Tuesday, three days after the launch, and for one shimmering weekend Amara Okafor was famous in her small world.

She did not see it first. The paper arrived at the newsagent's before dawn, and by the time Amara walked past on her way to school the man had already taped the front page to the inside of his window. She was not looking; she was doing what she did every morning, walking with her head down, counting paving stones, being the girl who was there but not there. Then she registered the shape in the glass — a girl in a heavy charcoal coat, a gold cardboard model held up to the light, an old man beside her looking at the sky — and she stopped so suddenly that the man behind her had to swerve.

LEWISHAM STUDENTS SEND WORDS TO THE STARS, the caption read, and underneath, smaller: Dr. E. Whitmore, retired astrophysicist, with student Amara Okafor at Saturday's launch from Cornwall. A project some called vanity. The photograph was grainier than the moment had been; in the paper the dawn was grey and the cardboard beetle had caught the flash and become a small gold explosion. She was smiling. She was actually, unmistakably smiling, with her chin up and her hair moving, and the girl in the photograph did not look like the girl who counted paving stones. She looked like somebody had told her the world was hers, and she had believed it for a second.

The newsagent came to the door. "That you, love?" She could not answer. "The kids from the school were in earlier. Patel bought three copies. Didn't say a word." He looked at the window, at her. "You done something, then."

"I wrote two lines," Amara said. It was the first time she had said it out loud to anyone but Whitmore. "They put them in a rocket."

He came back with a copy folded to the page and pressed it into her hands. "Take it. On the house. You want to keep a thing like that."

The school knew by break. She had told no one, but the paper was everywhere, spread open on the canteen tables, and Dev Patel had left one on the library desk with the photograph side up, and Mrs. Adeyemi had looked at it, and at Amara, and nodded once — the nod that said this book belongs to you by treaty. And the strange thing was not the nod. The strange thing was that the corridor, which had always flowed around Amara like water around a stone, began to flow through her instead.

"Oi, Okafor." A girl from the year above stopped her between lessons. "Is that really you? You went to Cornwall? For the space thing? That's actually mad."

"It's not mad," Amara said. "It's just—" But she had no word for what it was, and by lunchtime a boy she had never spoken to in four years said, "Saw you in the paper, yeah? Good on you." She understood that this was what visibility was: not fame, not glory, but the simple fact of being seen. Four years of perfecting invisibility, undone in a weekend by two lines and a photograph.

Jordan saw her in the corridor at the end of the day, leaning against the wall with his friends the way he had leaned at the winter concert, and Amara felt the old reflex — the drop of the eyes, the quickening step — and then she stopped. She did not stop to fight. She stopped because she understood she was not the same girl who had sat on the concrete steps in the February cold, and she wanted to see what it felt like to stand still in front of him. Jordan looked at her, and at the creased paper in her hand, and she saw him reach for the cruelty, the way you reach for a familiar tool. Then something happened she had not expected: he did not use it. He shrugged, one shoulder, almost an apology, and said, "You did all right, Okafor," and walked past, and the corridor was empty, and Amara stood very still and discovered she was shaking. She had braced all day for the winter concert to replay itself. It had not. The cruelty had failed to land, not because she had walked away, but because it had never come.

On the bus home she read the article. It was short, mostly engineering — the gravitational arc, the eight-million-year loop through the outer solar system, the seeds and soil samples sealed in vacuum canisters — and one sentence about the messages: students' handwritten words, chosen because ink and cellulose would outlast any digital format. And one sentence near the end that Amara read four times: Some have called the project vanity, a sentimental gesture in an age that cannot afford one. She felt something small and cold settle in her chest, the way the February cold had settled on the concrete steps, and she folded the paper so the sentence was hidden.

Grace was in the kitchen when Amara got home, which was unusual — Grace was always at work or asleep before a shift. But there she was, in her dressing gown with a cup of tea going cold, and the paper was open on the table, and the photograph page was the only page not neatly folded.

"Is this you?" Grace said. She did not look up. "The school trip. Cornwall. You told me it was a school trip."

"It was," Amara said. "We went to see the launch." She came slowly to the other side of the table.

"You wrote something," Grace said. "It says here you wrote something and they put it in the satellite. With the seeds." She finally looked up, and her eyes were red the way they got at the end of a double shift. "You wrote something, and you didn't tell me."

"I didn't think—" Amara began. "It was just two lines. You were asleep, you were always—" She stopped, because she heard what she was saying, and she did not want to say it.

Grace looked at the photograph for a long moment. She reached out and touched it once, with the back of her finger, the way you touch something to check it is real. Then she stood, went to the fridge, opened it, and said, without turning around: "Read it to me."

"What?"

"The lines. Read me your lines."

Amara stood in the kitchen with the tea going cold and the fridge door open and her mother's back to her, and she said the two lines out loud for the first time in her own home:

"What the perfect mind calls waste
is the soil where the future blooms."

The fridge hummed. And Grace said, still not turning around, her voice rough and low: "That's beautiful." And then, quieter: "That's my girl."

Amara had not cried at the launch. She had not cried at the winter concert. She stood in the kitchen with her mother's back to her, and she let the tears come, because there was no one in the room she needed to hide from. Grace closed the fridge door after a long time, went to her room, and slept. In the morning Amara found that her mother had cut the photograph out — carefully, with scissors — and left it on the table beside the cold cup of tea. Neither mentioned it, and Amara folded it into the pocket of the good charcoal coat, where it would live for the rest of her life.

The next Saturday, Whitmore telephoned the school and asked for Okafor, and Amara walked to the library and found the old man waiting with his cane and his grey eyes and the look of a man who had been carrying something for a long time.

"I want to show you where your words are going," he said.

The observatory was not what she had imagined. It was a squat concrete building on a hill in Greenwich, in the shadow of the great old observatory, used now for teaching and storage, full of the smell of dust and warm electronics. Whitmore had a key. The exile had never been quite complete; the people who ran the place remembered when he had been somebody, and they let him in after hours, and did not ask questions.

He led her up a narrow staircase to a room that was mostly ceiling. The ceiling was a dome, painted the deep blue of late evening, and across it, in thin white lines, ran the orbits — the planets in their ellipses, and one long looping curve that did not look like the others. It looked like a thrown stone. It rose from a small circle at one edge, swung out past the edge of the painted sky, and curved back, in a great slow bend, toward where it had begun.

"That's it," Whitmore said. "That's the Lament. That's where your words are going." His shaking finger travelled along the curve. "Out past Mars. Past the asteroids. Past Jupiter — they'll use its gravity to bend the arc — and out to the edge of the dark, and then, eight million years from now, back along this same curve. To whatever is standing in our place."

Amara stood under the painted dome and looked at the long white curve, and she tried to feel eight million years, and she could not. She could feel the cold step behind the gym. She could feel the skipping pen. But eight million years was not a feeling; it was a number, and it did not fit inside her chest.

"Will it come back to exactly here?"

"To within a few thousand kilometres," Whitmore said. "Which, at that distance, is like dropping a stone on the same pebble twice. The mathematics is very beautiful." He looked at her, and something in his face shifted. "The mathematics is beautiful. But it is not why they built it."

"Why did they build it?"

Whitmore was quiet for a long moment. He looked up at the painted dome, and when he spoke his voice was low, with the same tired brightness she had heard when he had said You have no idea what you've sent into the dark.

"Because it's a waste," he said. "Every engineer who worked on it knew it. Every auditor who signed off knew it. Eight million years, for twelve students' words and some seeds — a vanity, a sentimental gesture, a beautiful waste. They built it anyway. Do you know why? Because somebody has to. Because a species that only builds what it can account for has stopped believing there will be anybody after it. You build a message to the future because you believe the soil will bloom. Even when every account says it won't."

Amara thought of the sentence in the paper — a sentimental gesture in an age that cannot afford one — and she said, quietly: "You think they'll forgive it."

Whitmore's face went still, the way it went still when he was reading something true.

"No," he said. "I don't think they'll forgive it. I think that's the whole point." He looked at her, his grey eyes very tired and very kind. "The world is going to ask you to account for that waste one day. The perfect mind always does. It will ask what your two lines returned, what they were worth. And you will not have an answer that satisfies it, because a seed does not produce on demand. A seed produces in its own time, or not at all, and the perfect mind cannot wait, and so it will call your seed waste, and it will file it away. The world may not forgive a beautiful waste. I want you to know that now, while it is still shining on you, so that when it stops shining, you will know it was never about you. It was about whether the world could afford to believe in your lines. And the world usually decides it can't."

Amara stood under the painted dome, with her mother's folded photograph in the pocket of the good coat, and she heard the warning, and she understood it, and she did not believe it. That was the strange thing. She heard it the way you hear a weather forecast on a blue day, and she stood there under the painted stars and she chose — deliberately, knowingly, with her eyes open — to hope anyway.

"Eight million years is a long time to wait for a return," she said.

"It is," Whitmore said.

"But it's coming back," she said. "Whatever's there when it comes back will open it. It'll read it. And even if it calls it waste—" She felt the two lines move inside her, the way they had moved on the concrete step, the way they had moved on the headland. "Even if it calls it waste, it'll have had it. And that's not nothing. That's the whole point."

Whitmore looked at her for a long moment. His hands trembled at his sides. Then he did something he had never done: he reached out and took her hand, held it, and said, very quietly: "Yes. That's the whole point."

They stood together under the painted dome, looking at the long white curve of the thrown stone, and outside the real sky was coming dark, and somewhere out past the orbit of Jupiter the gold beetle was moving along that curve in silence, carrying her two lines and her mother's skipping blue ink, carrying the seeds and the soil and the sounds of the world.

Amara hoped all the way home on the bus. She hoped up the stairs of the flat — the lift was broken, it was always broken — and she stood at her window and took the folded photograph out of the good coat's pocket, and looked at the girl in the charcoal coat holding the gold model up to the light, the girl who was smiling, and she said the two lines to herself, once, like a prayer, or a curse, or a seed pressed into soil:

What the perfect mind calls waste
is the soil where the future blooms.

The weekend ended. Monday came, and the corridors went back to flowing around her — a little less than before, a little more kindly, but flowing around her all the same. The fame was over, as all such fame is over, and Amara went back to the library at lunch and sat in her chair by the window, and Mrs. Adeyemi did not stamp the eclipse book, and the world settled back into its ordinary shape.

But something had been planted. That was what the weekend had done: it had planted a small green shoot of knowing that she could be seen, that she could stand still in front of the world and not disappear, and that what the perfect mind calls waste was already, somewhere out past the orbit of Jupiter, blooming its slow way toward a future that did not exist yet. She did not know that in only a few years a global power would rise and name her seed waste and file her away. She did not know that the old man beside her under the painted dome had only a handful of years left. She knew only that it was spring, that she was visible, that her mother had called her lines beautiful, and that something she had made was out there in the dark, moving toward readers who had not been imagined.

And she hoped anyway. That was the whole point.

set.name: Amara Okafor
set.description: Now seventeen, early June, a few days after the Cornwall launch. For one shimmering weekend she was briefly famous in her small world: the local paper ran the photograph of her beside Whitmore holding the cardboard gold-foil model (Tuesday, three days after launch, caption 'LEWISHAM STUDENTS SEND WORDS TO THE STARS'), classmates stopped and spoke to her, and Jordan—who insulted her father at the winter concert—passed her in the corridor and said 'You did all right, Okafor' instead of striking. Dev Patel bought three copies of the paper and left one on the library desk photograph-side up. Her mother Grace read the couplet, called it beautiful, said 'That's my girl,' and cut the photograph out with scissors; Amara folded it into the pocket of the good charcoal coat, where she will carry it for the rest of her life. Whitmore took her to a small teaching observatory on a hill in Greenwich after hours and showed her the Lament's painted trajectory—a long white curve past Mars, Jupiter, out to the edge of the dark and back in eight million years—and warned her that the world may not forgive a beautiful waste, that the perfect mind will one day ask her to account for her two lines and file them away; she heard the warning and chose to hope anyway. She held Whitmore's hand under the painted dome. The fame faded by Monday; she is back to the library at lunch, renewing the eclipse book twelve times with Mrs. Adeyemi's nod, carrying the Lament Archive card and now the folded photograph. She does not know that the Atlas Concord will rise in two years and target the archive, nor that Whitmore has only a few years left. She is, for now, visible and hopeful.

set.name: Grace Okafor
set.description: Amara's mother, hospice nurse at Blackheath, works nights; still exhausted. This chapter she learned the truth about the 'school trip': she saw the newspaper photograph, read the couplet aloud at her own request, called it beautiful, and said 'That's my girl'—the flicker of pride Amara has needed for years. She cut the photograph out carefully with scissors and left it on the table for Amara, who folded it into the good coat's pocket. Neither of them spoke of it again. She does not know about the coming Atlas Concord or Whitmore's decline; she shows love through unspoken gestures.

set.name: Dr. Elias Whitmore
set.description: Elderly exiled astrophysicist, project lead of the Lament Archive, living alone in the Catford flat; his degenerative nerve condition continues (hands tremble; the tremors ease only in sleep). This chapter he took Amara to a small teaching observatory on a hill in Greenwich after hours (old colleagues still let him in), showed her the painted trajectory of the Lament through the outer solar system, and gave his warning: the perfect mind will ask her to account for her waste, the world may not forgive a beautiful waste, and a seed does not produce on demand. When she answered that even if the future calls it waste it will have had it, and that is the whole point, he took her hand and said 'Yes. That's the whole point.' He will continue to lead the Lament Archive until the Atlas Concord targets it; he has only a few years left.

set.name: Dev Patel
set.description: Amara's classmate, one of the twelve Lament Archive students. After the launch he bought three copies of the local paper and left one open on the library desk with the photograph of Amara facing up, saying nothing. Still loud and talkative by habit, privately moved; his word-list assignment is believed lost but he was once caught writing something in double chemistry. He does not yet know that the Concord's rise will lead him into the administrative corps.

set.name: Mrs. Adeyemi
set.description: School librarian at Lewisham Park Comprehensive. Saw the newspaper photograph of Amara and Whitmore and nodded once—the nod that says the eclipse book belongs to Amara by treaty. Unchanged otherwise.

set.name: Jordan
set.description: Boy from 4B, one of Dev Patel's orbit, who insulted Amara's absent father at the winter concert; his cruelty failed to land then. This chapter, seeing Amara in the corridor during her weekend of visibility, he reached for the cruelty and then did not use it—he shrugged, said 'You did all right, Okafor,' and walked past, an almost-apology. A minor background figure who may reappear.

Three days after the launch, the local paper ran the photograph of Amara beside Whitmore under 'LEWISHAM STUDENTS SEND WORDS TO THE STARS,' with a line about a project some called vanity. Grace cut the photograph out with scissors and left it on the table; Amara folded it into the pocket of the good charcoal coat. She will carry it for the rest of her life, through every later chapter, including the Concord years and the far-future reconstruction of her life.

Grace learned the 'school trip' was the Lament launch, asked Amara to read her the two lines aloud, called them beautiful, and said 'That's my girl'—the only flicker of pride Amara has ever clearly received from her. It matters later when Grace's death leaves Amara more alone (chapter 14) and when Amara revisits her life.

Whitmore took Amara to a small teaching observatory on a hill in Greenwich and showed her the Lament's painted trajectory: a long curve past Mars, Jupiter, out to the edge of the dark, and back in eight million years. He warned her that the perfect mind will one day ask her to account for her waste and file it away, and that the world may not forgive a beautiful waste; he told her it was never about her but about whether the world could afford to believe in her lines. She chose to hope anyway. This warning prefigures the Atlas Concord's rise and returns in the Concord chapters.

After the observatory, with the warning fresh, Amara deliberately chose to believe that even if the far future calls her lines waste, it will have had them—'That's not nothing. That's the whole point.' Whitmore took her hand and agreed. This conscious hope is the seed of her later refusal to file the archive away.

Two years after the launch, the Atlas Concord will rise: a global technocratic movement led by Praetor Lenore Voss, who believes hope must be allocated as a finite resource. Schools and ministries will begin to purge unproductive sentiment; Whitmore's funding will be threatened and the Lament Archive will be named as a target. (Outline chapter 6, 'The Shape of Efficiency.')

When the Atlas Concord rises, Whitmore's funding is threatened and the Lament Archive is officially named a target of the Ministry of Cultural Efficiency; Amara will watch the future she trusted start to close. (Outline chapters 6-7.)

chapters.name: The Shape of Efficiency
chapters.content:
The Atlas Concord did not arrive with soldiers, or tanks, or the sound of anything breaking. It arrived the way a tide does, and it arrived the way a door does: one Tuesday evening in June, in the voice of a woman with silver-grey hair, standing on a stage in a city Amara had never visited, while a caption at the bottom of every screen in the library said her name.

LENORE VOSS, it said. PRAETOR-DESIGNATE, ATLAS CONCORD.

Mrs. Adeyemi had left the wall screen on during a break in the shelving rota, which she would never have done in the old days, and the three of them — Amara, Mrs. Adeyemi, and a year-seven boy waiting for his mother — stood in the dim hush of the library and watched the woman speak. She was not young and not old. She wore a plain grey suit, no flag, no decoration, and she spoke without notes, in a voice that sounded like the answer to a question nobody had thought to ask.

"Hope is not free," Lenore Voss said. "It costs. It costs calories and classrooms and hospital beds. It costs the hours of the people who must deliver it, and the budgets of the people who must pay for it. And like every resource we have ever wasted, it must be measured, and it must be allocated, or it will be squandered on things that return nothing."

The year-seven boy looked up at Amara. "What's a praetor?" he whispered.

"I don't know yet," Amara said. It was the truest thing she said all summer.

On the screen, Voss was speaking about the shape of things: about how every civilization in history had died not from too little hope but from hope spent on the wrong places — on monuments, on vanity, on messages to futures that would never read them. The word vanity sat in Amara's chest like a pebble. She had read that word before, in a folded newspaper on the bus, two years ago, in a sentence about a project some called vanity. She had folded the paper so the sentence was hidden, and then her mother had cut the photograph out, and the photograph lived now in the pocket of the good charcoal coat, which hung now on the hook behind the library door because the summer was warm and she wore it less. But she still carried the photograph itself, folded small, in the pocket of whatever she wore, because some things you do not leave at home.

Mrs. Adeyemi switched the screen off. She did it without looking at it, the way you swat a wasp you have decided not to be stung by. She looked at the year-seven boy, then at Amara, and she said: "The new minister wants the library to do an audit."

"What kind of audit?" Amara said.

"The efficient kind." Mrs. Adeyemi's voice was flat. "They're asking every school to list the holdings that serve no measurable purpose. Fiction beyond the set texts. Poetry. Old atlases. The eclipse books." She did not look at Amara when she said the eclipse books, and Amara understood that the nod, the treaty, was being renewed in a new key. "They say it's not censorship. They say it's tidiness."

Amara stood very still behind the desk. Outside, the June light came through the tall windows in long yellow slabs, the way it had come through the windows of the corridor on the day Jordan had said You did all right, Okafor, and she thought of the shelf by the window, the one with the astronomy books, the eclipse book with the worn spine that she had renewed twelve times and would have renewed twelve hundred. She thought of her own two lines, sealed in a vacuum canister somewhere out past the orbit of Jupiter, and of the woman on the screen who had said that messages to futures that would never read them were vanity, and she felt, for the first time in two years, the future she had trusted begin to close, the way a door closes when you are still a step away from it.

She had been nineteen for a month. She had finished her A-levels in the spring — physics, maths, astronomy under the old syllabus that was already being quietly retired — and she had been offered a place to read astrophysics at a university in the north, and she had deferred it, because her mother's back was worse and the shifts were longer, and the Concord's first budget had already announced that places in the sciences would be rationed to those with "demonstrated civic return." Amara, who had spent four years learning to make herself invisible, did not know how to demonstrate return. So she shelved books for the summer and told herself it was temporary, and she kept the photograph in her pocket, and she did not tell anyone that she had once stood on a headland in Cornwall and been happy and visible and sure.

The Concord's doctrine arrived at the school in pieces, like a house being built around you while you sleep. In July there was an assembly about "emotional efficiency," and the head teacher — a tired man who had once let Whitmore speak in the library — stood at the front and said the words the Ministry had sent, and the students shuffled and yawned and understood nothing, and Amara sat in the back row and understood everything. In August the careers board was replaced with a board of "allocations," and the posters of universities and apprenticeships came down, and in their place went a chart of permitted futures, colour-coded by civic return, and Dev Patel stood in front of it for a long time with his hands in his pockets, reading the small print.

"Oi, Okafor," Dev said, when he found her in the library after closing, stacking chairs. He was twenty now, loud by habit, still the boy who had mocked the Lament Archive as pretty waste and then bought three copies of the paper and left one open on the desk with her photograph facing up, saying nothing. He had a new haircut and a new way of standing, and he was holding a folder with a seal on it that Amara did not recognize. "You've seen the allocations chart."

"I've seen it," Amara said.

"It's not stupid. I know you think it's stupid. But look — the planet's got eight billion people and a shrinking budget of everything, and we're still spending on things that make people feel nice and return nothing. Like —" He waved his hand, searching for the example that would land, and Amara felt the word coming before he said it, the way you feel rain coming. "Like the Lament."

Amara stopped stacking chairs.

"It's been two years, Okafor," Dev said, and his voice was not cruel, and that was the worst of it. "It's out there doing its loop. It'll come back in eight million years to a world that might not even be ours. And meanwhile there were kids in this school who — I'm not saying it wasn't beautiful. I'm saying it was beautiful and it did nothing, and we can't afford nothing anymore. That's all. That's the whole of it. The Concord's just the first ones honest enough to say it out loud."

"That's not the whole of it," Amara said. She heard her own voice come out steady, which surprised her. "Whitmore told you. A seed looks exactly like waste. It looks like nothing while it's in the ground. You can't audit a seed by what it returns in the quarter."

Dev looked at her, and something in his face flickered — the boy who had folded his word-list assignment carefully and kept it in his pocket, the boy who had been caught writing something in double chemistry and had gone red and hidden it. "It's not that I don't get it. It's that the world's changed, and people like us —" He stopped, and Amara understood that he had almost said people like us don't get to be beautiful, we have to be useful, and had swallowed it. "People like us are going to have to choose which side of the ledger we're on. I'm choosing the one that adds up."

"Does it?" Amara said.

Dev looked at her for a long moment. Then he shrugged, one shoulder, the way Jordan had shrugged in the corridor two years ago, and he said, "Ask me in ten years," and he walked out with the folder under his arm, and Amara stood among the half-stacked chairs and understood that she had just watched someone she knew walk through a door that was closing.

She took the 47 bus to Catford the next evening, because the warning had been in her chest all day, and she needed to stand somewhere it was true. The flat was the same as it had always been — the milk crate of books by the door, the single window looking onto the street, the kettle, the tremor — and Whitmore was smaller than she remembered, which she had not expected, because two years is a short time for a man to shrink. But his eyes were the same grey, tired and kind, and they lit when he saw her in the doorway.

"You've seen it, then," he said. "The shape of things."

"The Concord," Amara said. "It's everywhere. The school — the library — Dev —" She stopped. "Dev thinks it adds up."

Whitmore set the kettle to boil with his left hand, because his right was having one of its days. "Does it surprise you? He's young. He wants to matter. The Concord offers the arithmetic of mattering — you count, you're counted, you're accounted for. It's the oldest promise there is: give us your freedom to be wrong, and we will give you the dignity of being useful." He looked at her. "They offered me the same thing. A letter came last week."

"Who?"

"The Ministry of Cultural Efficiency. They're forming. That's their name — Cultural Efficiency. They wrote to the Lament Archive." Whitmore found an envelope on the sideboard and held it out, and Amara saw that his hand was shaking more than it had in February, more than it had under the painted dome. "They're auditing every project with an open telemetry budget. They asked for a statement of return. They asked what the Lament has produced in two years that can be weighed, counted, or filed. And then —" He took the letter back and folded it, carefully, with both hands, the way a man folds something he means to keep. "And then they named us. In the public statement. The Lament Archive is on the list of projects recommended for closure. A vanity project. A beautiful waste."

Amara sat down in the chair by the window without being asked. "What will you do?"

"I'll answer them," Whitmore said. "I'll take the seeds — I'll take photographs of the vault, the sterilized soil samples, the DNA bank, the audio. I'll show them that a seed is a thing you can weigh. I'll argue that the payload is data, real data, catalogued and redundant and recoverable, and I will watch them not believe me, because it is not the payload they object to." He poured the tea with his steadying left hand, and it trembled anyway, and a little slopped onto the saucer. "They object to the handwriting. They object to the hope. The Ministry of Cultural Efficiency does not want to burn the seeds, Amara. It wants to file the word waste next to the word hope and be done with it. That is the new cruelty. Not fire. Tidiness."

"But the trajectory," Amara said. "It's already moving. Nobody can file away something that's already out there."

Whitmore looked at her over the steam of his cup, and his face went still the way it went still when he was reading something true. "No," he said. "Nobody can stop the satellite. The gold beetle is past the orbit of Mars by now; I checked the telemetry this morning before the letter. It does not know there is a Ministry. It does not know there is a doctrine. It is doing the only thing it ever did, which is carrying your two lines through the dark at a speed no committee can audit." He set the cup down. "But they can stop us from ever telling anyone it matters. They can make the telemetry unreachable. They can make the Archive a word you are embarrassed to say. That is how a thing dies now — not by burning, but by being filed so deep that nobody remembers it was lit."

Amara thought of the painted dome in Greenwich, of the long white curve of the thrown stone, of the girl in the photograph who had looked like somebody had told her the world was hers. Two years. It had been two years since the headland, and the world had changed its shape while she was shelving books, and the warning the old man had given her under the painted stars — the world may not forgive a beautiful waste — had been a forecast, and the blue day was over.

"Amara." Whitmore's voice was gentle. "I need you to hear me, because I may not be the one to tell you this later. The Ministry will come for the Archive. They may come for me. They may even come for you, because you are the girl in the photograph, the handwriting behind the lines. When they do, they will ask you to account for it, and you will give them two lines, and they will file them. Do not let that make you believe the lines were nothing. Do you understand me? A seed is not measured by what the auditor sees. It is measured by what grows."

"And if nothing grows?" Amara said.

Whitmore was quiet for a long moment, and the kettle ticked, and the summer light came grey through the single window. "Then it was still planted," he said. "And the planting was not waste. The planting was the whole point. Say it back to me."

Amara looked at him, at the shaking hands and the tired grey eyes, and she said the two lines out loud, slowly, the way you say a thing to keep it true: "What the perfect mind calls waste is the soil where the future blooms."

Whitmore nodded. "Good. Now go home and tell yourself that every time they make you feel small. The Concord will build a machine for making people feel small, and you will live inside it for the rest of your life, and you must not let it teach you that a waste is never an investment. That is the sentence I would give my whole life to leave behind me, and you are the one carrying it now."

Amara did not know, standing in the doorway of the Catford flat with her hand on the latch, that she would carry that sentence for more than fifty years. She did not know that the letter he had folded so carefully was the first official document of a war the Archive would lose, or that the Ministry would come for him before the year's end, or that the painted dome would be painted over, or that the good charcoal coat would one day be the coat she wore to stand on the perimeter of a rally. She knew only that the old man had put the weight of the Archive into her hands, and that she had accepted it, and that somewhere past the orbit of Mars the gold beetle was still moving along its long white curve, carrying her two lines through the dark, and no ministry on Earth could reach it.

She said goodnight and walked down the stairs of the Catford flat and out into the summer evening, and the street was full of people who did not know that the shape of the world had changed, and Amara, who had learned to be invisible, walked among them with her hands in her pockets, one hand closed around the folded photograph, and felt the future she had trusted closing like a door behind her, and kept the two lines inside her like a seed she had promised to carry.

That autumn, the Ministry of Cultural Efficiency published its first efficiency ledger, and on page forty-seven, under the heading "Projects Deemed Unable to Demonstrate Civic Return," the Lament Archive was listed by name, with a single line of annotation: seed vault, DNA bank, audio and image payload, and twelve handwritten student messages. Payload retained for archival storage; ongoing telemetry operations not recommended for further allocation. The notification was written so plainly that it took Amara three reads to understand that it was an ending. She read it in the school library, where Mrs. Adeyemi had mimeographed copies for the staff, and she thought of the headland in Cornwall, of the gold model held up to the light, of the woman with the radio, of the twelve students standing in the wind, and she folded the page and put it in the pocket of the good charcoal coat, beside the photograph, where it would live. She did not know yet that the Ministry's word for what had happened to her was deprioritization, and that deprioritization was the shape efficiency took when it wanted to erase a thing without the mess of burning it. She knew only that the future she had trusted had started to close, and that she had promised an old man she would carry the waste in her pocket until someone remembered it was soil.

And she kept the promise. That was the whole point.

set.name: Amara Okafor
set.description: Now nineteen, a month past her birthday, summer two years after the Cornwall launch. Finished A-levels in physics, maths, astronomy in the spring; was offered a place to read astrophysics at a university in the north and deferred it because her mother's back is worse and the Concord's first budget rationed science places by 'demonstrated civic return'—which she, trained in invisibility, does not know how to demonstrate. Shelves books at the school library for the summer and tells herself it is temporary. Still carries the folded newspaper photograph in the pocket of the good charcoal coat, and now also carries the folded Ministry efficiency-ledger page (page 47, 'Projects Deemed Unable to Demonstrate Civic Return') that names the Lament Archive. Watched Lenore Voss's Concord announcement on the library screen; heard Dev Patel say 'we can't afford nothing anymore'; visited Whitmore in Catford and accepted the weight of the Archive from him, promising to carry his sentence that a waste is never an investment. She knows the Archive has been named for closure but not yet that the Ministry will disband it, reclassify its telemetry, and come for Whitmore before the year's end, nor that the painted dome will be painted over. She feels the future she trusted closing like a door behind her and keeps the two lines inside her like a seed she has promised to carry.

set.name: Grace Okafor
set.description: Amara's mother, hospice nurse at Blackheath; still works nights, now with a worsening back and longer shifts, which is the stated reason Amara deferred university. Her flicker of pride over the couplet (chapter 5) stands; she and Amara have not spoken of it since. She does not know about the Concord's rise or the Ministry's targeting of the Lament Archive. Shows love through unspoken gestures; the folded photograph her daughter carries was cut out by her hands.

set.name: Dr. Elias Whitmore
set.description: Elderly exiled astrophysicist, project lead of the Lament Archive, living alone in the Catford flat. Two years older and visibly smaller; his right hand has bad days and his left trembles when pouring tea. Still has old colleagues who let him check the Lament's telemetry: he confirmed this chapter that the gold beetle is past the orbit of Mars and beyond any committee's reach. Received a letter from the newly forming Ministry of Cultural Efficiency asking for a statement of return and naming the Lament Archive on a list of projects recommended for closure; he folded and kept the letter, and told Amara he will answer the Ministry with the payload's real data (seeds, DNA bank, audio and images) while knowing they object not to the payload but to the handwriting and the hope. He gave Amara the sentence he means to leave behind: 'a waste is never an investment,' and told her the new cruelty is tidiness, not fire—things die by being filed too deep to remember they were lit. He will defend the Archive before the efficiency tribunal next chapter; he has only a few years left.

set.name: Dev Patel
set.description: Twenty years old, one of the twelve Lament Archive students, still loud by habit, now with a new haircut and a new way of standing. Standing before the school's new colour-coded 'allocations' chart in August, he told Amara the Concord is 'the first ones honest enough' to say that beauty that does nothing can no longer be afforded, and that people like them must choose which side of the ledger they are on—'I'm choosing the one that adds up.' When she answered with Whitmore's seed argument he said 'Ask me in ten years.' He carries a folder with an unfamiliar seal and is moving toward the new administrative corps, though he has not formally joined yet. Privately still the boy who folded his word-list assignment and kept it in his pocket.

set.name: Mrs. Adeyemi
set.description: School librarian at Lewisham Park Comprehensive. Told Amara the new minister wants an audit of holdings serving no measurable purpose—fiction beyond set texts, poetry, old atlases, 'the eclipse books'—framed as tidiness, not censorship; her flat voice and her refusal to look at Amara when saying 'the eclipse books' renew her old treaty with Amara in a new key. She switched off the library screen during Voss's announcement and mimeographed the Ministry's efficiency ledger for the staff, through which Amara saw the Archive named.

set.name: Lenore Voss
set.description: Praetor-designate of the Atlas Concord, a global technocratic movement rising in June, two years after the Lament launch. Silver-grey hair, plain grey suit, speaks without notes in a voice that sounds like the answer to a question nobody thought to ask. Doctrine: hope is not free; it costs calories, classrooms, hospital beds, and budgets, and must be measured and allocated like any resource or it will be squandered on things that return nothing—monuments, vanity, messages to futures that will never read them. Believed by her movement to be 'the first ones honest enough to say it out loud.' Will preside over the rise of the Ministry of Cultural Efficiency and the purge of unproductive sentiment.

In the spring of her A-level year, Amara was offered a place to read astrophysics at a university in the north but deferred it: her mother Grace's back was worse and the Concord's first budget rationed science places to those with 'demonstrated civic return,' which Amara, trained in invisibility, could not demonstrate. She shelved books at the school library for the summer and told herself it was temporary. This deferral shapes her path into librarianship and the Concord years.
